name: Marijuana rescheduling to Schedule III
where_it_stands: Marijuana covered by a state medical license, and FDA-approved marijuana drugs, have been in Schedule III since 28 April 2026; all other marijuana, including adult-use, is still Schedule I. Written argument in the DEA hearing on moving all marijuana to Schedule III closed on 5 November, so the administrative law judge can now issue his recommendation, while a consolidated lawsuit against the April order is being briefed in the D.C. Circuit.

next_milestone.text: Challengers' consolidated opening brief due in the D.C. Circuit lawsuit against the April order, under the schedule the parties jointly proposed; the DEA judge's recommendation on full rescheduling has no deadline and could come first.

summary: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche used the treaty-based scheduling power in the Controlled Substances Act to move a slice of marijuana into Schedule III without a full rulemaking: FDA-approved marijuana drug products and marijuana handled under a state medical marijuana license. The same order created a fast-track DEA registration pathway for state medical licensees and launched a new hearing, which began on 29 June 2026, on the 2024 proposal to move all marijuana to Schedule III. The hearing's final briefs, on how much weight a GAO report about scheduling procedures deserves, were filed on 5 November; Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius will send a non-binding recommendation to the DEA Administrator, who makes the final decision. Separately, opponents including Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a drug-testing trade group and the attorneys general of Indiana and Nebraska are challenging the April order in the D.C. Circuit, which has refused to pause it.

what_changes.text: State medical licensees can register with the DEA and operate as Schedule III handlers; registration only covers what the state license allows and lapses automatically if that license is suspended or expires. Adult-use operations remain Schedule I.

The order treats a state medical certification that meets basic content rules as enough for a dispensary to supply a patient, so registered patients are no longer buying a Schedule I drug. Federal workplace testing and other collateral rules have not automatically changed.

For medical activity, Section 280E no longer applies from the 2026 tax year according to Treasury, but mixed medical and adult-use businesses still await IRS apportionment guidance, and the order faces a pending court challenge.
Recreational buyers see no federal change: adult-use marijuana stays Schedule I until the separate hearing and any final rule conclude.

timeline.event: DOJ proposes moving all marijuana to Schedule III through regular rulemaking
President Trump signs an executive order directing the Attorney General to finish moving medical marijuana to Schedule III
DOJ announces the order placing FDA-approved and state-licensed medical marijuana in Schedule III and sets a new hearing on full rescheduling
Order published in the Federal Register and takes effect
New DEA administrative hearing on broader rescheduling begins
Judge Julius refuses to reopen the hearing over a GAO report but admits it and allows short briefs
DEA and opponents file final reply briefs, ending the stay on the judge's recommendation

faq.a: Only partly. Marijuana in an FDA-approved drug or covered by a state medical marijuana license moved to Schedule III on 28 April 2026. Everything else, including adult-use cannabis, remains in Schedule I.

faq.q: Does Schedule III make recreational marijuana federally legal?
faq.a: No. Even if all marijuana moved to Schedule III, making or selling it outside the federal registration and prescription system would still be a federal crime, according to the Congressional Research Service.

faq.q: When will the DEA decide on full rescheduling?
faq.a: There is no deadline. The judge can now write his recommendation after final briefs closed on 5 November 2026; the DEA Administrator then makes the final decision, which can be contested.

faq.q: Is the April order being challenged in court?
faq.a: Yes. Three consolidated petitions are before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which declined to stay the order. The parties proposed finishing briefing by February 2027.
